name: Canis Major
introduction: is the Great Dog, following Orion across the sky. It is home to Sirius, the brightest star in the night sky, which makes the dog easy to find: follow the line of Orion’s Belt southeast. It is best seen on northern winter evenings.

sections.title: What makes it special
paragraphs: [Sirius](hip:32349) shines brightly mainly because it is so close: only about 8.6 light-years away. In ancient Egypt, its first appearance in the dawn sky signaled the annual Nile flood. To the Greeks and Romans, its rising with the Sun coincided with the hottest weeks of summer, which is why we still call them the “dog days”.

Sirius has a secret companion. In 1844, Friedrich Bessel noticed that Sirius wobbles as it moves across the sky, revealing an unseen partner. In 1862, Alvan Graham Clark found it: [Sirius B](id:sirius-b), a white dwarf with about the mass of the Sun packed into a sphere the size of Earth.

sections.title: Notable stars
paragraphs: The other bright stars of the Great Dog are distant giants. [Adhara](hip:33579) is the brightest source of extreme ultraviolet light in our sky. About 4.7 million years ago, when it was much closer to the Sun, it was the brightest star in the night sky, far brighter than Sirius is today.

[Wezen](hip:34444) is a yellow-white supergiant about 1,600 light-years away, and [Aludra](hip:35904) a blue supergiant even farther away. [Mirzam](hip:30324), whose name means “the announcer”, rises just before Sirius and heralds its appearance.

sections.title: Beyond the stars
paragraphs: The open cluster M41 is visible to the naked eye about four degrees south of Sirius. Farther away are VY Canis Majoris, a red hypergiant and one of the largest stars known, and Thor’s Helmet, a bubble of gas blown by a powerful Wolf–Rayet star.
